ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, above the dashed line at a height of $h=0.8\mathrm{m}$ from the horizontal ground, there is a uniform magnetic field directed horizontally into the plane of the paper. The square wire frame abcd has a side length of $l=0.2\mathrm{m}$, a mass of $m=0.1\mathrm{kg}$, and a resistance of $R{=}0.08\Omega$. The frame is initially thrown vertically upward with a certain initial velocity. When the $ab$ side of the frame enters the magnetic field with a velocity of $v_{0}=2\mathrm{m/s}$, a constant upward force $F=2\mathbf{N}$ is applied to the frame, causing it to move at a constant velocity. After the entire frame enters the magnetic field, the external force $F$ is immediately removed. The frame continues to rise in the magnetic field for some time before it begins to fall and eventually lands on the ground. The acceleration due to gravity is taken as $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. The magnitude of the magnetic induction intensity of a uniform magnetic field
2. The time it takes for the wire frame to enter the magnetic field from the start until it reaches the highest point.
3. The magnitude of the velocity when the wireframe lands.
4. The Joule heat generated by the wireframe during the entire process.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, above the horizontal dashed line there are multiple “×” marks, indicating that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper inward; the height from the dashed line to the horizontal ground below is labeled h. The square wire frame abcd is located near the dashed line, the top side ab is entering the magnetic-field region, and above the wire frame there is a vertically upward velocity arrow v0. Below the wire frame there is a ground line, and on the left side a double-headed arrow marks the height h. Reasoning: When the wire frame enters the magnetic field upward, the area passing through the magnetic field changes, an induced current is produced, and the magnetic force opposes the motion, with direction downward. The external force F is upward and makes the wire frame enter at uniform speed v0, so the forces are balanced: F=mg+F_B, where F_B=B^2l^2v0/R. Substitute F=2 N, m=0.1 kg, g=10 m/s^2, l=0.2 m, v0=2 m/s, R=0.08 Ω: mg=1 N, therefore 2=1+B^2·(0.2)^2·2/0.08=1+B^2, giving B=1 T. The time required for the wire frame to completely enter the magnetic field is t1=l/v0=0.2/2=0.1 s. After it completely enters the uniform magnetic field, the magnetic flux no longer changes, and there is no induced current. After the external force is removed, it is acted on only by gravity, and the time required to rise to the highest point is t2=v0/g=2/10=0.2 s. Therefore the total time from the start of entering the magnetic field to the highest point is t=t1+t2=0.3 s. When falling, during the stage in which it is completely within the uniform magnetic field there is no induced current; when it reaches the lower boundary and starts to leave the magnetic field, the speed magnitude is again v0=2 m/s. During the process of leaving the magnetic field, at v0 the magnitude of the magnetic resistance is B^2l^2v0/R=1 N, equal to the gravity mg, therefore the wire frame passes through the boundary at uniform speed. After completely leaving the magnetic field, the height of the lower side of the wire frame above the ground is h-l=0.8-0.2=0.6 m, and it undergoes free fall downward at 2 m/s; the landing speed v=sqrt(v0^2+2g(h-l))=sqrt(4+12)=4 m/s. Joule heat is produced only when entering and leaving the magnetic field. The electric power each time is P=(Blv0)^2/R=(1·0.2·2)^2/0.08=2 W, and each duration is l/v0=0.1 s, so the total heat Q=2Pt=2×2×0.1=0.4 J.
